reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Chapter 8 addresses structural aspects and limit states for driven pile foundations per AASHTO (2014) LRFD specifications. Factored structural resistance must exceed factored loads. Topics include driving stress limits, group layout, preliminary cap design, in-service stress limits, and buckling. Material-specific provisions govern structural pile design: concrete (Article 5), steel (Article 6), and timber (Article 8).
sections.body: (pp. 427-428) Piles resist vertical loads, moments and lateral loads; this chapter covers the pile's structural limit states, which can govern where lateral and axial loads act together, as vessel impact, wind, scour and earthquake loads often do (chapter introduction, p. 427). It is not a full structural design treatment; see AASHTO (2014). A driven pile must pass stress and buckling checks under static design loads and under driving, so material limits are compared with factored driving stresses and factored design loads. The highest stresses almost always occur in driving, needed to overcome the nominal geotechnical plus dynamic resistance; the high strain rate and short duration allow a substantially higher driving stress limit than for static design. Wave equation analysis predicts driving stresses before installation and dynamic testing monitors them during it. Factored loads are in Chapter 2; AASHTO (2014) covers concrete piles in Article 5, steel in Article 6, timber in Article 8, and concrete filled steel pipe. Factored structural resistance depends on (1) average section yield strength (Fy for steel and reinforcement, f'c typically at 28 days, wood crushing strength), (2) timber factors for incision, loading rate, submersion, shape and analysis method, (3) the resistance factor phi_i, and (4) the load factor gamma_i. The chapter covers driving stress limits, group layout, preliminary cap design, in-service stress limits and buckling.

sections.title: Basic Structural Properties of Driven Piles
sections.summary: Primary pile materials are steel, concrete, and timber; each significantly affects nominal structural and driving resistance. Steel elastic modulus E_s = 29,000 ksi; concrete modulus E_c = 1820*sqrt(f'c) (Eq. 8-1); timber properties vary by species. Moment of inertia formulas are provided for solid circular, hollow circular, and solid square sections. Elastic section modulus S = I/c is used for moment-induced stress evaluation; H-pile and pipe pile section properties tabulated in Figures 8-1 through 8-3.

sections.title: Material Properties
sections.summary: Steel pipe piles (ASTM A-252) have yield stress from 35 to 80 ksi; H-piles (ASTM A572) require minimum Fy = 50 ksi — A-36 grade is no longer manufactured. Concrete elastic modulus E_c = 1820*sqrt(f'c) (Eq. 8-1) for normal weight concrete. Timber species reference values: Douglas-Fir (Fco=1.25 ksi, Eo=1500 ksi), Southern Pine (Fco=1.20 ksi, Eo=1500 ksi), Red Oak (Fco=1.10 ksi, Eo=1250 ksi), Red Pine (Fco=0.90 ksi, Eo=1280 ksi).
sections.body: (pp. 428-430) Steel, concrete and timber properties strongly affect static nominal structural resistance and nominal driving resistance. Steel piles are produced to a minimum yield stress (Table 8-1 pipe: ASTM A-252 Grade 2, 35 ksi; Grade 3, 45 ksi; Grade 3 (Mod), 50-80 ksi. Table 8-2 H-piles: A-36, 36 ksi; ASTM A-572-50, 50 ksi; A-572-60, 60 ksi). ASTM A572 requires new H-pile sections at a minimum of 50 ksi, so A-36 H-piles are no longer made. Es = 29,000 ksi for static calculations (AASHTO 2014). For concrete the modulus and strength limit, reinforcement adds tensile strength, and without test data AASHTO estimates the modulus by Eq. 8-1 (normal weight concrete, 145 pcf). Timber properties vary by species: Douglas-Fir and Southern Pine predominate, with Red Oak and Red Pine also used; AASHTO (2014) Article 8.4.1.4 reference values (Table 8-3) are modified by shape and size factors (Section 8.4).

sections.title: Pile Section Definitions
sections.summary: Pile shape and element dimensions govern axial compression and flexural resistance modes. Moment of inertia formulas: solid circular I = pi*D^4/64 (Eq. 8-2), hollow circular I = pi*(D^4-D1^4)/64 (Eq. 8-3), solid square I = b^4/12 (Eq. 8-4). Elastic section modulus S = I/c (Eq. 8-5) is used to evaluate moment-induced stresses. H-pile dimensions and section properties are in Figures 8-1 and 8-2 (pipe pile dimensions in Figure 8-3); sections should be selected from locally available stock to avoid scheduling delays.
sections.body: (pp. 430-433) Shape and element dimensions govern how much force can be transferred in driving or service and the axial and flexural resistance; Figures 8-1 and 8-3 give H-pile and pipe pile dimensions and Figure 8-2 H-pile section properties. The largest stresses occur farthest from the neutral axis (outer edge of a pile, outermost piles of a group), so area, moment of inertia and edge distance are needed for combined axial and flexural checks. Moment of inertia comes from Eqs. 8-2 to 8-4, or AISC (2011) shape tables or Figure 8-2 for H-piles (strong and weak axis); the elastic section modulus from Eq. 8-5. Choose sections locally available, as suppliers do not stock every size.

sections.title: Effective Length and Buckling
sections.summary: Piles act as columns with effective length factor K from end conditions (Figure 8-4: design K 0.65, 0.80, 1.0, 1.2, 2.1, 2.0); the toe is usually fixed. Buckling matters through water, air or liquefied soil; load tests (Bethlehem Steel 1970) and Coduto et al. (2016) indicate even very soft soils prevent underground buckling under axial load. LPILE analysis (Chance 2003) is a more conservative check.
sections.body: (pp. 433-434) Piles act as columns; end conditions give the effective length factor K (Figure 8-4), with the toe generally fixed in translation and rotation. Without sufficient bracing (very soft soils, piles through water, large scour) the head may sway and the design K should be used; a pier cap subject to severe scour may give fixed rotation with free translation, and a bent cap may differ along and across its axis. Rollins and Stenlund (2010): for a rotationally fixed head, design the cap connection (embedment and reinforcement) to exceed the pile moment capacity rather than use a rule of thumb embedment. Buckling matters through water or air or in liquefaction, and concern has been raised for very soft soils or peat, but it depends on confining stress and load (Davisson 1963). Bethlehem Steel Corporation (1970) load tests: an H-pile through 31 ft of water and 29 ft of organic silt, where it sank under its own weight, settled 0.63 in. under 200 tons (0.02 in. net) without buckling; Coduto et al. (2016): even the softest soils prevent underground buckling under axial load, especially with a cap fixing the head. Chance (2003) gives a more conservative approach, finding the critical buckling load with software such as LPILE under incremental loads. Figure 8-4 design K values: 0.65, 0.80, 1.0, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.0 (theoretical 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 2.0).

sections.title: Structural Considerations and Resistance Factors
sections.summary: AASHTO (2014) nominal static design stress limits represent resistance consistently achievable with traditional driving equipment. Under LRFD, factored resistance must exceed factored loads (phi*Rn >= sum(eta_i*gamma_i*Q_i)). Factored loads are defined in AASHTO Article 3; driving stress limits are in material-specific articles: concrete (Art. 5), steel (Art. 6), timber (Art. 8). Resistance factors are applied to nominal structural resistance to obtain factored design resistance for each limit state.
sections.body: (pp. 434-435) Code limits on nominal static design stresses generally reflect the static resistance that traditional driving equipment and methods can consistently develop. Factored resistance must exceed factored loads, and the AASHTO limits for factored design stresses generally keep driving stresses within limits. Factored loads: AASHTO Article 3; driving stress limits: Articles 5 (concrete), 6 (steel) and 8 (timber).
key_points: Factored resistance must exceed factored loads per LRFD methodology
AASHTO factored pile design stress limits keep driving stresses within recommended limits
Factored loads defined in AASHTO Article 3 (load combinations)

sections.title: Depth to Fixity
sections.summary: Unbraced length is the distance between braced points resisting buckling. For piles through air or water, depth to fixity d_f approximates the effective column length for preliminary lateral analysis. For clay: d_f = 1.4*(E*Iw/Es)^0.25 (Eq. 8-6), where Es = 0.465*su (Eq. 8-7). For sand: d_f = 1.8*(E*Iw/nh)^0.2 (Eq. 8-8), using nh from Table 8-4. If a p-y lateral pile analysis has been performed, the depth-to-fixity concept is unnecessary.
sections.body: (pp. 435-436) AASHTO (2014) defines the unbraced length l as the distance between two braced points resisting buckling or distortion; for embedded piles it covers scour and stickup through air or water. For preliminary analysis with lateral load, the effective length for flexural or torsional resistance is the total unsupported length plus an embedded depth to fixity; after a p-y lateral analysis (Chapter 7) the concept is unnecessary, and most lateral software also finds buckling capacity. Preliminary depth to fixity: Eqs. 8-6 and 8-7 for clays, Eq. 8-8 for sands with nh from Table 8-4 (loose 0.417 dry or moist, 0.208 submerged; medium 1.110, 0.556; dense 2.780, 1.390 ksi/ft).

sections.title: Limiting Slenderness Ratio
sections.summary: For piles with an unbraced length through air or water, slenderness must be checked under axial compression. Non-composite steel piles must satisfy Kl/rs <= 120 (Eq. 8-9), where K is the effective length factor (Figure 8-4), l is the unsupported length plus depth to fixity, and rs = sqrt(I/A) is the minimum radius of gyration. Fully embedded piles are braced by soil and do not require a slenderness check.
sections.body: (p. 436) Piles through air or water are unbraced over some length, so the slenderness ratio should be checked for axial compression; non-composite steel piles not fully embedded must satisfy Eq. 8-9.
key_points: Check slenderness where piles extend through air or water

sections.title: Resistance Factors
sections.summary: AASHTO (2014) LRFD resistance factors applied to nominal structural resistance: Pr = phi_c*Pn (Eq. 8-13), Mr = phi_f*Mn (Eq. 8-14), Vr = phi_v*Vn (Eq. 8-15). Driving factors: phi_da = 1.0 for steel and concrete; 1.15 for timber. Structural factors from Table 8-6: steel H-pile axial phi_c = 0.60 (good conditions)/0.50 (severe); steel pipe phi_c = 0.70/0.60; combined axial+flexural phi_c = 0.70 (H-pile)/0.80 (pipe); flexure phi_f = 1.00 for steel; timber compression phi_c = 0.90, flexure phi_f = 0.85.
sections.body: (pp. 436-438) Sections 8.4 to 8.7 give step by step nominal structural resistance for timber, steel and concrete piles per AASHTO (2014); under LRFD a resistance factor is applied and the factored load must not exceed the factored resistance. Load combinations (Chapter 2) give the factored axial, moment and shear loads (Eqs. 8-10 to 8-12) and the factored resistances are Eqs. 8-13 to 8-15. Table 8-5 gives driving resistance factors (steel and concrete 1.0, timber 1.15) and Table 8-6 structural factors. The text's example: a steel H-pile with good driving conditions and a pile tip (point or shoe) uses phi_da = 1.0 in Eq. 8-33 and phi_c = 0.60 in Eq. 8-34; Table 8-6 lists 0.60 for H-piles where a pile tip is not necessary and 0.50 where it is.

sections.title: Timber Piles
sections.summary: Timber piles are round, tapered, and suited for modest loading levels; Douglas Fir and Southern Pine are the most common species in the US. Reference design values (Table 8-7) include Fco, Fbo, Fvo, and Eo. Adjusted resistance uses modification factors including format conversion C_KF = 2.5/phi, wet service C_M = 1.0, size factor C_F (Eq. 8-16), and time effect C_lambda: 0.8 (Strength I), 1.0 (Strength II/III), 0.6 (Strength IV), 1.0 (Extreme Event I) per Table 8-8.
sections.body: (pp. 439-440) Timber piles are round, tapered and used for modest loads; Douglas Fir and Southern Pine are by far the most common in the U.S. Table 8-7 reference values (Fco, Fbo, Fvo, Eo) are modified by adjustment factors for the load case and pile. The time effect factor C_lambda (Table 8-8) depends on limit state: AASHTO commentary uses Strength I where cumulative live load duration is two months, Strength II for less, and Strength IV for permanent loads. The size factor CF applies in flexure only where the critical section exceeds 12 in. diameter (area 144 in^2), by Eq. 8-16 with b the side of a square of equal area (Showalter 2012), else 1.0. A wet service factor CM = 1.0 is recommended; the volume, incising, deck and flat-use factors (Cv, Ci, Cd, Cfu) are taken as 1.0 for piles in the manual.

sections.title: Driving Stresses
sections.summary: Timber pile driving may cause shearing or brooming near the pile top; stress concentrations also develop as the tapered section decreases toward the toe. AASHTO (2014) limits the maximum driving stress to sigma_dr = phi_da * (2.6 * Fco) (Eq. 8-17), where phi_da = 1.15 for timber and Fco is the reference compression stress parallel to grain (Table 8-7). This limit applies to both compression and tension driving stresses.
sections.body: (pp. 440-441) Timber piles should be installed so as to avoid excessive stresses that shear or broom the head; stresses may also rise along the pile as the taper narrows toward the toe. AASHTO (2014) limits compression and tension driving stress by Eq. 8-17 with phi_da = 1.15.

sections.title: Structural Resistance
sections.summary: Timber pile structural resistance per AASHTO (2014) covers axial compression (Pr = phi*Pn, phi = 0.9, Eq. 8-18) and flexure (Mr = phi*Mn, phi = 0.85, Eq. 8-26). Adjusted compression: Fc = Fco*C_KF*C_M*C_F*C_i*C_lambda (Eq. 8-19); format conversion factor C_KF = 2.5/phi_c. Column stability factor C_p (Eq. 8-22) accounts for buckling when bracing is insufficient. Combined flexure and axial compression interaction (Eq. 8-30) must be satisfied when both loads are present.
sections.body: (p. 441) AASHTO (2014) Articles 8.6, 8.8 and 8.10 give the axial and flexural resistance limits of timber; the checks below use Table 8-7 reference values, Table 8-8 time effect factors and Eq. 8-16, with factors not pertaining to piles taken as 1.0: axial compression parallel to grain (8.4.2.1), flexure (8.4.2.2) and combined flexure and axial compression (8.4.2.3).

Eq. 8-29: Mn = Fb S; S = elastic section modulus (in^3); Fb = adjusted resistance in flexure (ksi) (p. 444)

sections.title: Combined Flexure and Axial Compression
sections.body: (p. 444) Combined loading must satisfy the beam rupture and lateral buckling check of Eq. 8-30, with FcE and E from Eqs. 8-31 and 8-32; if it fails, an alternative pile design is required.
key_points: Eq. 8-31: FcE = KcE E b^2 / Le^2; Eq. 8-32: E = Eo CM Ci
If the check fails, an alternative pile design is required
equations: Eq. 8-30: (Pu / Pr)^2 + Mu / [Mr (1 - Pu / (FcE Ag))] <= 1.0; Pr from Eq. 8-18; Pu from Eq. 8-10; Mr from Eq. 8-26; Mu from Eq. 8-11; Ag = gross area (in^2) (p. 444)
Eq. 8-31: FcE = KcE E b^2 / Le^2; KcE = 0.76; b = pile width or diameter (in.); Le = KL (Figure 8-4) (in.) (p. 444)
Eq. 8-32: E = Eo CM Ci; CM and Ci = 1.0 for piles; Eo from Table 8-7 (p. 444)
sections.applicability: Combined axial and flexural check of timber piles.

sections.title: Steel Piles
sections.summary: Steel piles sustain higher driving stresses than concrete or timber; compression stress limit is sigma_dr = 0.9*Fy (phi_da = 1.0, Eq. 8-33). Tensile yielding does not typically occur during driving, so no tension limit is required. Primary types are H-piles and pipe piles. Structural checks per AASHTO Articles 6.9.4 and 6.12.2.2 cover axial compression, flexure, combined loading, and shear. Slender element factor Q and torsional buckling apply to H-piles extending through air or water.
sections.body: (p. 445) Steel pile driving stresses are Section 8.5.1, structural resistance 8.5.2 (axial compression, flexure, combined axial compression and flexure, shear) and a worked HP 14x117 example 8.5.3.
key_points: Steel piles handle highest driving stresses among pile materials
Driving stress limit governed by yield strength; only compression limit needed
Primary types: H-piles and pipe piles
Structural checks: axial compression, flexure, combined axial/flexure, and shear
Slender element reduction factor Q may apply for local buckling
Both flexural and torsional buckling modes must be checked for H-piles
sections.applicability: Overview of structural design for steel H-piles and pipe piles.

sections.title: Driving Stresses
sections.summary: Steel pile driving stresses are limited to compression only; tensile stresses during driving do not typically yield steel piles. Maximum compression driving stress: sigma_dr = phi_da * (0.9 * Fy) (Eq. 8-33), where phi_da = 1.0 for steel piles (Table 8-5). Yield stress Fy ranges from 35 to 80 ksi for pipe piles (ASTM A-252, Table 8-1) and from 36 to 60 ksi for H-piles (Table 8-2).
sections.body: (p. 445) Steel piles take higher driving stresses than concrete or timber, limited by yield strength (Table 8-1); higher grades may be specified. Driving does not usually generate tension high enough to yield steel, so only a compression limit is needed: Eq. 8-33 with phi_da = 1.0.
key_points: Maximum driving stress: sigma_dr = phi_da * (0.9 * Fy)
phi_da = 1.0 for steel piles (Table 8-5)
Compression driving stress only; tension limit not required
Fy = yield stress of steel (Table 8-1 for pipe, Table 8-2 for H-piles)
equations: Eq. 8-33: sigma_dr = phi_da (0.9 Fy), steel compression driving stress limit; phi_da = 1.0 (Table 8-5); Fy = yield stress of steel (Table 8-1) (ksi) (p. 445)
sections.applicability: Steel pile driving stress limit.

sections.title: Structural Resistance
sections.summary: Steel pile structural resistance follows AASHTO Articles 6.9.4 and 6.12.2.2. Factored axial: Pr = phi_c*Pn (Eq. 8-34; phi_c = 0.60 for H-piles, 0.70 for pipe). Nominal axial uses inelastic buckling Pn = Po*0.658^(Po/Pe) (Eq. 8-43, Pe/Po >= 0.44) or elastic Pn = 0.877*Pe (Eq. 8-44). H-pile flexure depends on flange slenderness (lambda_f vs lambda_pf/lambda_rf); pipe pile flexure on D/t ratio. Combined axial-flexure: Eq. 8-57 (Pu/Pr < 0.2) or Eq. 8-58 (Pu/Pr >= 0.2).
sections.body: (p. 445) Steel pile structural resistance covers axial compression (8.5.2.1), flexure (8.5.2.2), combined axial compression and flexure (8.5.2.3) and shear (8.5.2.4), following AASHTO (2014) Articles 6.9.4 and 6.12.2.2; Section 8.5.3 works an HP 14x117.
key_points: Factored axial resistance: Pr = phi_c * Pn (Eq. 8-34)
Factored flexural resistance: Mr = phi_f * Mn (Eq. 8-45)
Nominal axial resistance considers yield (Po) and elastic buckling (Pe)
Sections: axial 8.5.2.1, flexure 8.5.2.2, combined 8.5.2.3, shear 8.5.2.4; example 8.5.3
sections.applicability: Steel pile structural resistance.

sections.title: Axial Compression
sections.body: (pp. 445-448) The factored resistance is Eq. 8-34; the nominal resistance considers strength and buckling. Step 1: the equivalent nominal yield resistance Po = Q Fy Ag (Eq. 8-35), Q = 1.0 for non-slender piles (slender members: AASHTO Article 6.9.4.2.2); the local buckling check is Eq. 8-36 with Eq. 8-37 for H-piles and Eq. 8-38 for unfilled pipe. Step 2: the elastic critical buckling resistance Pe (Section 8.2.3): flexural buckling (Eq. 8-39) for fully embedded piles, and for doubly symmetric open sections (H-piles) through water or air also torsional buckling (Eqs. 8-40 to 8-42), the lesser governing. Step 3: Pn by Eq. 8-43 if Pe/Po >= 0.44, else Eq. 8-44 (AASHTO Article 6.9.4.1).
key_points: Eq. 8-34: Pr = phi_c Pn (Table 8-6)
Eq. 8-35: Po = Q Fy Ag; Q = 1.0 for non-slender piles
Eq. 8-36: bf/(2 tf) <= 0.64 sqrt(kc Est / Fy), 0.35 <= kc <= 0.76; Eq. 8-37: kc = 4 / sqrt(dw/tw)
Eq. 8-38: unfilled pipe D/t <= 0.11 Est / Fy
Eq. 8-39: Pe = pi^2 Est Ag / (K l / rs)^2 (flexural buckling)
Eq. 8-40: torsional buckling for H-piles through water or air; Eq. 8-41 Cw = Iy h^2/4; Eq. 8-42 G = 0.385 Est
Eq. 8-43: Pn = Po 0.658^(Po/Pe) if Pe/Po >= 0.44; Eq. 8-44: Pn = 0.877 Pe otherwise
equations: Eq. 8-34: Pr = phi_c Pn; phi_c from Table 8-6 (p. 445)
Eq. 8-35: Po = Q Fy Ag; Po = equivalent nominal axial yield resistance (kips); Q = slender element reduction factor (1.0 for non-slender piles; AASHTO Article 6.9.4.2.2) (p. 446)
Eq. 8-36: bf / (2 tf) <= 0.64 sqrt(kc Est / Fy), with 0.35 <= kc <= 0.76, H-piles; bf = flange width; tf = flange thickness (in.); Est = elastic modulus of steel (ksi) (p. 446)
Eq. 8-37: kc = 4 / sqrt(dw / tw); dw = web depth; tw = web thickness (in.) (p. 446)
Eq. 8-38: D / t <= 0.11 Est / Fy, unfilled pipe piles; D = pipe diameter; t = wall thickness (in.) (p. 447)

Eq. 8-39: Pe = pi^2 Est Ag / (K l / rs)^2, flexural buckling; Pe = elastic critical buckling resistance (kips); K = effective length factor (Figure 8-4); l = unbraced length in the plane of buckling (in.); rs = radius of gyration about the axis normal to the plane of buckling (in.) (p. 447)

Eq. 8-40: Pe = [pi^2 Est Cw / (Kz lz)^2 + G J] Ag / (Ix + Iy), torsional buckling of doubly symmetric open sections; Cw = warping torsional constant (in^6); Kz, lz = effective length factor and unbraced length for torsional buckling; G = shear modulus (ksi); J = St. Venant torsional constant (in^4); Ix, Iy = major and minor axis moments of inertia (in^4) (p. 447)
Eq. 8-41: Cw = Iy h^2 / 4; h = distance between flange centroids (in.) (p. 448)
sections.applicability: Axial compression resistance of steel H and pipe piles.

sections.title: Flexure
sections.body: (pp. 449-452) The factored flexural resistance is Eq. 8-45; the procedure covers H-piles (and I-sections) and pipe piles only (other sections: AASHTO Article 6.12.2.2). A. H-sections: Step 1, flange slenderness lambda_f (Eq. 8-46) and the compact and non-compact limits (Eqs. 8-47, 8-48); Step 2, Mn = Mp (Eq. 8-49) with Mp = 1.5 Fy Sy about the weak axis (Eq. 8-50) if lambda_f <= lambda_pf, or Eq. 8-51 if lambda_pf < lambda_f <= lambda_rf. B. Pipe piles: Step 1, if D/t <= 0.07 Est/Fy (Eq. 8-52) the plastic moment governs (Step 2a, Eq. 8-53), otherwise local buckling (Step 2b, the text says 'Equation 8-2' here): Eq. 8-54 if D/t <= 0.31 Est/Fy, else Eq. 8-55 with fcr from Eq. 8-56.
key_points: Eq. 8-45: Mr = phi_f Mn (Table 8-6: phi_f = 1.00 for steel)
Eqs. 8-46 to 8-48: lambda_f = bf/(2 tf); lambda_pf = 0.38 sqrt(Est/Fyf); lambda_rf = 0.83 sqrt(Est/Fyf)
Eqs. 8-49, 8-50: compact flange Mn = Mp = 1.5 Fy Sy (weak axis)
Eq. 8-51: non-compact flange, Mn reduced linearly between Mp and the Sy term
Eq. 8-52: pipe D/t <= 0.07 Est/Fy, then Eq. 8-53 Mn = Mp = Fy Zy
Eq. 8-54: Mn = [0.021 Est/(D/t) + Fy] Sy for D/t <= 0.31 Est/Fy
Eqs. 8-55, 8-56: Mn = fcr Sy, fcr = 0.33 Est/(D/t) for D/t > 0.31 Est/Fy
equations: Eq. 8-45: Mr = phi_f Mn; phi_f from Table 8-6 (p. 449)
Eq. 8-46: lambda_f = bf / (2 tf); flange slenderness ratio (p. 449)
Eq. 8-47: lambda_pf = 0.38 sqrt(Est / Fyf); limiting slenderness ratio for a compact flange; Fyf = minimum yield strength of the lower strength flange (ksi) (p. 449)
Eq. 8-48: lambda_rf = 0.83 sqrt(Est / Fyf); limiting slenderness ratio for a non-compact flange (p. 449)
Eq. 8-49: Mn = Mp, if lambda_f <= lambda_pf (p. 450)
Eq. 8-50: Mp = 1.5 Fy Sy, HP-sections about the weak axis; Sy = elastic section modulus about the weak axis (in^3) (p. 450)

Eq. 8-51: Mn = [1 - (1 - Sy / Zy)((lambda_f - lambda_pf) / (0.45 sqrt(Est / Fyf)))] fyf Zy, if lambda_pf < lambda_f <= lambda_rf (weak axis); Zy = plastic section modulus about the weak axis (in^3) (p. 450)
Eq. 8-52: D / t <= 0.07 Est / Fy; if satisfied the plastic moment governs (Step 2a), otherwise local buckling (Step 2b) (p. 451)
Eq. 8-53: Mn = Mp = Fy Zy (p. 451)
Eq. 8-54: Mn = [0.021 Est / (D / t) + Fy] Sy, if D/t <= 0.31 Est / Fy (p. 452)
Eq. 8-55: Mn = fcr Sy, if D/t > 0.31 Est / Fy (p. 452)
Eq. 8-56: fcr = 0.33 Est / (D / t); fcr = elastic local buckling stress (ksi) (p. 452)
sections.applicability: Flexural resistance of steel H and pipe piles.

sections.title: Combined Axial Compression and Flexure
sections.body: (pp. 452-453) Combined checks apply only to groups of vertical piles; AASHTO (2014) has no recommendation for battered piles. Eq. 8-57 applies if Pu/Pr < 0.2, Eq. 8-58 if Pu/Pr >= 0.2. Table 8-6 uses phi_c = 0.70 (H) and 0.80 (pipe) for combined axial and flexural loading of undamaged piles.
key_points: Applies to groups of vertical piles; no AASHTO recommendation for battered piles
Eq. 8-57: Pu/(2.0 Pr) + (Mux/Mrx + Muy/Mry) <= 1.0 if Pu/Pr < 0.2
Eq. 8-58: Pu/Pr + (8.0/9.0)(Mux/Mrx + Muy/Mry) <= 1.0 if Pu/Pr >= 0.2
Combined loading: phi_c = 0.70 H-piles, 0.80 pipe piles (Table 8-6)
equations: Eq. 8-57: Pu / (2.0 Pr) + (Mux / Mrx + Muy / Mry) <= 1.0, if Pu/Pr < 0.2; Pu = factored axial load (kips); Pr from Section 8.5.2.1; Mux, Muy = factored moments and Mrx, Mry = factored flexural resistances about x and y (kip-ft) (p. 453)
sections.applicability: Combined axial and flexural check of steel piles.

sections.title: Shear
sections.body: (pp. 453-454) Bridge foundation piles are generally not used for high shear, since large lateral deflections hurt serviceability. The factored shear resistance is Eq. 8-59; for an H-pile Vn = C Vp (Eq. 8-60, C typically 1.0) with Vp = 0.58 Fyw dw tw (Eq. 8-61). Significant shear or other non-composite sections: see AASHTO (2014).
key_points: Bridge piles generally not used to resist high shear (serviceability)
Eq. 8-59: Vr = phi_v Vn (phi_v = 1.00 steel)
Eq. 8-60: Vn = C Vp, C typically 1.0 for H-piles; Eq. 8-61: Vp = 0.58 Fyw dw tw
equations: Eq. 8-59: Vr = phi_v Vn; phi_v from Table 8-6 (p. 453)
Eq. 8-60: Vn = C Vp; C = ratio of shear-buckling resistance to shear yield strength, typically 1.0 for H-piles (p. 453)
Eq. 8-61: Vp = 0.58 Fyw dw tw; Vp = plastic shear force (kips); Fyw = web yield strength (ksi); dw = web depth; tw = web thickness (in.) (p. 453)
sections.applicability: Shear resistance of steel H-piles.

sections.title: Example Calculations for H Pile Structural Resistance
sections.summary: Worked example for HP14x117 pile (Fy=50 ksi, A=34.4 in^2, rs=3.59 in) with scour-induced unbraced length l=120 in (K=1.2). Non-slender check (Eq. 8-36) gives Q=1.0; Po=1720 kips, Pe=6120 kips, Pe/Po=3.56 >= 0.44 governs inelastic buckling; Pn=1529 kips, Pr=917 kips (phi_c=0.60). Flange slenderness lambda_f = 9.25 lies between lambda_pf = 9.15 (printed once as 9.25) and lambda_rf = 19.98, so Eq. 8-51 gives Mn = Mr = 4555 kip-in (phi_f = 1.0). Factored shear resistance Vr=332 kips.
sections.body: (pp. 454-458) An HP 14x117 for an integral abutment: Fy = 50 ksi, Est = 29,000 ksi, weak axis rs = 3.59 in. (Figure 8-2), unbraced length l = 120 in. for scour, rotation fixed and translation free at the head and both fixed at the toe, so K = 1.2 (Figure 8-4); Kl/r < 120. kc = 4/sqrt(14.2/0.805) = 0.952, limited to 0.76; Eq. 8-36: 14.9/(2 x 0.805) = 9.25 <= 13.44, so Q = 1.0. Po = 1.0 x 50 x 34.4 = 1720 kips; Pe = 6120 kips; Pe/Po = 3.56 >= 0.44, so Eq. 8-43 gives Pn = 1529 kips and, with phi_c = 0.60 (good driving, no toe protection; 0.70 in the combined equations), Pr = 917 kips. Flexure: lambda_f = 9.25; lambda_pf is printed as 9.25 when computed and as 9.15 in the comparison 9.15 < 9.25 <= 19.98 and in Eq. 8-51; lambda_rf = 19.98. The text says 'Equation 8-48 will be used' but applies Eq. 8-51 with Sy = 59.5 in^3 and Zy = 91.4 in^3: Mn = 4555 kip-in, Mr = 4555 kip-in (phi_f = 1.0). Shear: dw = 14.2 in., tw = 0.805 in., Vp = 0.58 x 50 x 14.2 x 0.805 = 332 kips = Vn = Vr (phi_v = 1.0).

Vp = Vn = Vr = 332 kips (phi_v = 1.0)

sections.title: Concrete Piles
sections.summary: Concrete piles are strong in compression; tensile strength is provided by reinforcing and prestressing steel. Nearly all concrete piles manufactured today are prestressed, enabling larger tensile stress capacity. Unlike steel and timber, concrete piles are susceptible to damage in both compression and tension during driving. Pile cushions are used to slow impact velocity and reduce peak dynamic forces. Driving stresses are applied to the gross concrete section area.
sections.body: (p. 459) Concrete pile driving stresses are Section 8.6.1 and structural resistance 8.6.2 (axial compression, biaxial flexure).
key_points: Concrete strong in compression; tensile strength from reinforcing/prestressing steel
Nearly all concrete piles manufactured today are prestressed
Susceptible to damage in both compression and tension during driving
Pile cushions used to reduce dynamic forces during driving
Driving stresses applied to gross concrete area
sections.applicability: Overview of structural design considerations for concrete driven piles.

sections.title: Driving Stresses
sections.summary: Both compression and tension driving stresses must be checked for concrete piles per AASHTO (2014). Compression limit: sigma_dr = phi_da*(0.85*f'c - f_pe) (Eq. 8-62). Tension limit: sigma_dr = phi_da*(0.095*sqrt(f'c) + f_pe) (Eq. 8-63). Resistance factor phi_da = 1.0; effective prestress f_pe = 0.5 to 1.0 ksi typical for highway piles. In severe corrosive environments, tension is limited to the effective prestress after losses.
sections.body: (p. 459) Concrete is strong in compression and relies on reinforcing and prestressing steel for tension; prestressing, used in nearly all U.S. concrete piles, allows larger tensile stresses. Unlike timber and steel, concrete piles can be damaged in compression or tension in normal driving; pile cushions (Chapter 15) slow impact velocity and reduce dynamic forces. Limits apply to the gross concrete area; in severely corrosive environments tension is limited to the effective prestress after losses. AASHTO (2014): Eq. 8-62 (compression) and Eq. 8-63 (tension), phi_da = 1.0. fpe (AASHTO Chapter 10 designation) is typically 0.5 to 1.0 ksi for highway piles and should certainly be less than f'c.
key_points: Compression driving stress: sigma_dr = phi_da * (0.85*f'c - f_pe)
Tension driving stress: sigma_dr = phi_da * (0.095*sqrt(f'c) + f_pe)
phi_da = 1.0 for concrete piles (Table 8-5)
f_pe = effective prestressing stress, typically 0.5 to 1.0 ksi for highway piles
f_pe must be less than f'c
Severe corrosive environments: tension limited to the effective prestress after losses
equations: Eq. 8-62: sigma_dr = phi_da (0.85 f'c - fpe), concrete compression driving stress limit; phi_da = 1.0 (Table 8-5); fpe = effective prestressing stress in concrete (ksi) (p. 459)
Eq. 8-63: sigma_dr = phi_da (0.095 sqrt(f'c) + fpe), concrete tension driving stress limit (p. 459)
sections.applicability: Concrete pile driving stress limits.

sections.title: Structural Resistance
sections.summary: Concrete pile structural resistance per AASHTO covers axial compression and biaxial flexure. Factored axial: Pr = phi_c*Pn (Eq. 8-64). Nominal axial with spiral reinforcement: 0.85 factor (Eq. 8-65); tie reinforcement: 0.80 factor (Eq. 8-66). Biaxial flexure: reciprocal method (Eq. 8-68) when Pu >= 0.10*phi*f'c*Ag; moment ratio (Eq. 8-70) when lower. Resistance factors: tension-controlled RC phi_c=0.90, PS compression phi_c=0.75, PS tension phi_c=1.00. FB-Pier generates 3D interaction failure surfaces.
sections.body: (p. 460) Concrete pile structural resistance covers axial compression (8.6.2.1) and biaxial flexure (8.6.2.2).
key_points: Axial compression 8.6.2.1; biaxial flexure 8.6.2.2
sections.applicability: Concrete pile structural resistance.

sections.title: Axial Compression
sections.body: (p. 460) The factored resistance is Eq. 8-64. The nominal resistance is Eq. 8-65 for spiral reinforcement or Eq. 8-66 for ties; the 0.85 and 0.80 factors allow for unintended eccentricity (AASHTO commentary; details AASHTO Article 5.7.4.4).
key_points: Eq. 8-64: Pr = phi_c Pn (Table 8-6)
Eq. 8-65: spiral Pn = 0.85 [0.85 f'c (Ag - Astr - Aps) + Fyr Astr - Aps (fpe - Est epsilon_cu)]
Eq. 8-66: ties, factor 0.80 in place of 0.85
Factors allow for unintended eccentricity (AASHTO Article 5.7.4.4)
equations: Eq. 8-64: Pr = phi_c Pn; phi_c from Table 8-6 (p. 460)

Eq. 8-65: Pn = 0.85 [0.85 f'c (Ag - Astr - Aps) + Fyr Astr - Aps (fpe - Est epsilon_cu)], spiral reinforcement; fpe = effective stress in the prestressing steel after losses (ksi); Fyr = yield stress of reinforcing steel (ksi); Astr = longitudinal reinforcement area; Aps = prestressing steel area (in^2); Est = elastic modulus of prestressing steel; epsilon_cu = concrete failure strain in compression (p. 460)
Eq. 8-66: Pn = 0.80 [0.85 f'c (Ag - Astr - Aps) + Fyr Astr - Aps (fpe - Est epsilon_cu)], tie reinforcement (p. 460)
sections.applicability: Axial compression resistance of prestressed and reinforced concrete piles.

sections.title: Biaxial Flexure
sections.body: (pp. 461-464) The factored flexural resistance is Eq. 8-67; biaxial checks (AASHTO Article 5.7.4.5) are Eq. 8-68 with Eq. 8-69 if Pu >= 0.10 phi f'c Ag, and Eq. 8-70 otherwise. The response of a prestressed section to axial load and two moments is complex; FB-Pier assumes stress-strain relationships with maximum concrete strength 0.85 f'c (all points reduced to 85 % for loading time), builds biaxial interaction diagrams for increasing axial loads up to axial failure (Figure 8-5: an 18 in. solid square pile, 16 strands, f'c = 8 ksi, effective prestress 1200 psi), and stacks them into a three dimensional failure surface; a load case is checked by whether its force vector (axial, Mx, My) falls inside. The program also handles steel piles and concrete filled pipe.
key_points: Eq. 8-67: Mr = phi_f Mn
Eq. 8-68: 1/Prxy = 1/Prx + 1/Pry - 1/(phi Po) <= 1.0 if Pu >= 0.10 phi f'c Ag (Eq. 8-69 for the axial term)
Eq. 8-70: Mux/Mrx + Muy/Mry <= 1.0 if Pu < 0.10 phi f'c Ag
FB-Pier: stacked interaction diagrams form a 3-D failure surface; check whether the force vector lies inside
Figure 8-5: 18 in. solid square pile, 16 strands, f'c = 8 ksi, effective prestress 1200 psi
equations: Eq. 8-67: Mr = phi_f Mn; Mr, Mn in kip-ft; phi_f from Table 8-6 (p. 461)

Eq. 8-68: 1 / Prxy = 1 / Prx + 1 / Pry - 1 / (phi Po) <= 1.0, if Pu >= 0.10 phi f'c Ag; Prx, Pry = factored axial resistance with only ey or only ex present; Prxy = factored axial resistance with biaxial flexure (kips) (p. 461)
Eq. 8-69: Pn = 0.85 f'c (Ag - Astr - Aps) + Fyr Astr - Aps (fpe - Est epsilon_cu) (printed as Pn for the Po of Eq. 8-68) (p. 461)
Eq. 8-70: Mux / Mrx + Muy / Mry <= 1.0, if Pu < 0.10 phi f'c Ag; moments in kip-in (p. 461)
sections.applicability: Biaxial flexure of prestressed concrete piles.

sections.title: Composite Piles
sections.summary: Composite piles are defined as concrete-filled steel pipe piles per AASHTO (2014). Requirements: steel area >= 4% of total, concrete f'c = 3.0 to 8.0 ksi, reinforcing Fy <= 60 ksi. Driving stresses evaluated as non-composite steel (Section 8.5.1). Nominal axial resistance uses normalized slenderness factor lambda (Eq. 8-72): Pn = 0.66^lambda * Fe * Ast (Eq. 8-76) when lambda <= 2.25; Pn = 0.88*Fe*Ast/lambda (Eq. 8-77) when lambda > 2.25. Section properties Fe (Eq. 8-73) and Ee (Eq. 8-74) account for composite action.
sections.body: (p. 464) For structural purposes composite piles are concrete filled steel pipe piles; AASHTO (2014) gives no guidance for others (e.g., concrete with an H-pile stinger), whose resistance along each length should be evaluated for the primary material there. Driving stress is Section 8.7.1 and structural resistance 8.7.2.
key_points: Composite piles = concrete filled steel pipe piles per AASHTO (2014)
Driving stresses evaluated as non-composite steel section (Section 8.5.1)
Other composites (e.g., concrete with H-pile stinger): evaluate each length for its primary material
sections.applicability: Structural design of concrete filled steel pipe piles per AASHTO (2014).

sections.title: Driving Stress
sections.body: (p. 464) Concrete filled pipe piles are driven unfilled, so the non-composite steel driving stresses of Section 8.5.1 apply.
key_points: Driven unfilled: use the steel driving stress limit (Section 8.5.1)
sections.applicability: Driving stress of concrete filled pipe piles.

sections.title: Structural Resistance
sections.body: (p. 464) Composite structural resistance is treated as axial compression (Section 8.7.2.1).
key_points: Axial compression of concrete filled pipe: Section 8.7.2.1
sections.applicability: Structural resistance of concrete filled pipe piles.

sections.title: Axial Compression
sections.body: (pp. 464-466) AASHTO (2014) composite methods apply if (1) steel is at least 4 % of the total area (otherwise treat as non-composite by Section 8.6), (2) f'c is between 3.0 and 8.0 ksi (lower limit to encourage good concrete), and (3) the longitudinal reinforcement yield strength used does not exceed 60.0 ksi. The factored resistance is Eq. 8-71. Step 1: lambda from Eq. 8-72 (taken as 0 if fully embedded) with Eqs. 8-73 to 8-75 (C1 = 1.00, C2 = 0.85, C3 = 0.40 for concrete filled pipe). Step 2: Pn by Eq. 8-76 if lambda <= 2.25 or Eq. 8-77 if lambda > 2.25 (the text says 'Equation 8-73 or Equation 8-74').
key_points: Steel area >= 4 % of total, else non-composite (Section 8.6)
f'c between 3.0 and 8.0 ksi; reinforcement yield used <= 60.0 ksi

sections.title: Layout of Pile Groups
sections.summary: Pile group layout begins with estimating pile count as factored axial load divided by single pile resistance, rounded up ~15% (Eq. 8-78). Minimum center-to-center spacing is 2.5 ft or 2.5D per AASHTO; 3.0D recommended. Trial layout is checked using the Rigid Cap Method (Eq. 8-79): Pui = (Puz+Wc+Ws)/n + Mux*y/sum(y^2) + Muy*x/sum(x^2). Maximum single pile load must not exceed factored structural resistance. Software (GROUP, FB-Pier) using t-z and p-y curves provides refined soil-structure interaction analysis.
sections.body: (pp. 467-469) Large loads need a pile group, whose initial layout is needed for in-service stress checks under the AASHTO Article 3.4 load combinations (loads in Figure 8-6). Software such as GROUP or FB-Pier distributes loads with t-z and p-y curves; alternatively the rigid cap method is done by hand. Step 1: estimate the number of piles (Eq. 8-78), dividing the factored axial load by the factored geotechnical resistance of one pile and rounding up (say by 15 % or more, by the moments and lateral loads); lateral or tension loads may govern and need more piles. Step 2: trial configuration; AASHTO (2014) minimum center-to-center spacing is the lesser of 2.5 ft or 2.5 diameters, but experience shows 3.0 diameters is a more practical minimum (CRSI Design Handbook 2002 has example layouts). Step 3: maximum single pile load by Eq. 8-79 for all factored load combinations, not just the largest axial; if it exceeds the factored structural resistance add piles or widen spacing and recompute; an unsymmetrical cap may suit unequal moments.

Eq. 8-79: Pui = (Puz + Wc + Ws) / n + Mux y / sum(y^2) + Muy x / sum(x^2), rigid cap method with equal pile stiffness; Pui = maximum single pile factored axial load (kips); Puz = factored axial load on the cap (kips); Wc = cap weight; Ws = soil weight above the cap (kips); Mux, Muy = factored moments on the cap (kip-ft); x, y = distances from the column center to each pile (ft) (p. 468)

sections.title: Preliminary Design of Pile Bent and Group Caps
sections.summary: Preliminary pile cap sizing follows AASHTO LRFD concrete design. Estimated cap thickness: t_cap = Pui/12 + 30 inches (Eq. 8-80). Effective shear depth dv = tcap - dc - ds - df (Eq. 8-81), not less than max(0.9*ds, 0.72*h). Design checks include two-way punching shear around column (Eqs. 8-87/8-88) and individual piles, one-way beam shear (Eqs. 8-93/8-94), and cap flexural resistance (Eq. 8-97). Minimum pile embedment 12 inches; minimum spacing 30 inches or 2.5D; edge cover 9 inches.
sections.body: (pp. 470-481) Guidelines for a preliminary cap size for cost estimating; full structural and seismic design is outside the manual. The CRSI Design Guide for Pile Caps (Mays 2015, following ACI (2014), piles with nominal loads up to 400 tons, with spreadsheets) helps develop a preliminary cap for AASHTO design. A bent cap is designed like a pier cap (Wilson et al. 2006), with added issues of pile embedment, structural depth, cover, misalignment tolerance, anchorage and spacing; design is iterative. Plan size per AASHTO Article 10.7.1.2: spacing at least 30.0 in. or 2.5 diameters and at least 9 in. from cap edge to pile side. Thickness is embedment plus clear space plus structural depth; piles project at least 12.0 in. into the cap after damaged material is removed, or 6.0 in. with embedded bars or strands. Shear failures: punching about one pile, a pair of piles, a pile at a corner, and the column. Step 1: trial thickness by Eq. 8-80 (including embedment and 3 in. clear space). Step 2: dv by Eq. 8-81 (not less than the greater of 0.9 ds or 0.72 h, AASHTO 5.8.2.9, and for preliminary sizing may be taken as that value; Figure 8-7) and the column punching perimeter bo (Eqs. 8-82 to 8-84). Step 3: two-way shear at dv/2 from and at the column face (Figure 8-8) and around piles (Figures 8-9, 8-10): Vu by Eq. 8-85 or 8-86, Vn by Eqs. 8-87 to 8-90 (AASHTO 5.13.3.6.3; the text cites Eqs. 8-84 and 8-85 here), Vr by Eq. 8-91, check Eq. 8-92. Step 4: one-way shear (AASHTO 5.13.3.6.2, 5.8.3.2; Figures 8-11, 8-12): Vu by Eq. 8-93, Vn the lesser of Eqs. 8-94 and 8-95 (the text says Eqs. 8-91 or 8-92), Vr = phi_v Vn, check Eq. 8-96. Step 5: bending, Eq. 8-97, with Mn from Eqs. 8-98 and 8-99 (after AASHTO 5.7.3.2.2-1); taking d - a/2 = 0.9d gives a preliminary steel area, refined by one more cycle; reinforcement should develop Mr of at least 1.33 times the factored moment (AASHTO 5.7.3.3.2). The step heading in the print repeats 'Layout of Pile Groups'.

sections.title: Cap Considerations for Large Pile Sizes
sections.summary: For Large Diameter Open-Ended Piles (LDOEPs), the general pile cap design procedure from Section 8.9 applies. No strict AASHTO guidance exists for minimum spacing and embedment of large pile sizes; most state agencies lack standard plans. Case studies (Brown and Thompson 2014) show pile tops embedded approximately 3 feet into pier caps. Minimum center-to-center spacing of approximately 3 pile diameters is recommended, consistent with drilled shaft group layout guidelines.
sections.body: (p. 481) For large diameter open-ended piles (LDOEPs) follow the general steps above; no strict guidance exists on spacing and embedment, and most agencies lack standard plans. Case studies in Brown and Thompson (2014 in the text; the references list 2015) embedded pile tops about 3 ft into the pier cap, more than for smaller piles. Spacing should follow drilled shaft guidance given comparable diameters; the plan in Brown and Thompson shows a minimum of about 3 diameters center to center, consistent with drilled shaft group layouts (Brown et al. 2010).
